baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Treats the interview as evidence produced through a relationship
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The adapted 1991 excerpt, section IV, describes questions, changing relationships and the distortion caused by removing the interviewer’s voice. The handout modernizes bracketed terms and is not an exact 1981 transcription.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Uses displaced chronology to examine narrated meaning without changing event dates
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The adapted excerpt, section III, uses workers’ memories of Trastulli in Terni to distinguish event chronology from narrated meaning. Factual verification remains necessary; false memories do not replace established dates.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Portelli and the Phokeng project make testimony an interpreted source for everyday lives
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Testimony changes the evidence available for everyday lives; interpretation must include narration and the interview relationship. The Phokeng introduction places material relations alongside narratives rather than treating experience as transparent.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Life-history inquiry expands access to experiences while questioning homogeneous group identities
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Interview projects may expand participation, but interviewees are not transparent representatives of homogeneous groups. Bozzoli’s introduction connects women’s narratives to differentiated social positions; representation is an analytical question.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Oral-history inquiry makes recollection’s meanings and social organization research questions
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Portelli treats the meanings of recollection and narrative difference as evidence, not merely as errors to correct. Passerini’s retrospective account qualifies collective memory and discusses everyday negotiation; Frisch’s contents add public mediation as a reading route. Assmann’s 1995 discussion explicitly draws on oral-history research and Niethammer when describing communicative memory. This is an additional named reception alongside Portelli and Passerini, not a common founding doctrine.
